extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing stand-up comedians and humor writers
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance on the major joke/formula structures used in stand-up comedy, with examples and notes on delivery, tags, and audience reaction. Focused on crafting bits, punchlines, act-outs and building comedic stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying framework / Setup and shatter the assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying framework of all the formulas is to set up an assumption and shatter the assumption — create surprise by making the audience think you will say/do one thing, then do another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic mechanism across formulas: establish an expectation, then break it for the laugh. Use misdirection, reversal, or an absurd third item to shatter the implied framework. Apply across bits, stories and acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOUBLE ENTENDRES
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays on words that include cliché reformations and take-offs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a phrase with an obvious meaning and reveal an alternate, risqué or unexpected meaning. Example: John McKay’s press-conference reply “I’d be okay with that.” Can be adapted to scripts and many subjects. Watch for clarity so the double meaning is perceived by the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: REVERSES
rubrics_metrics.description: Trick the audience by a last-second switch in point of view — set up an image or expectation then flip it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a detailed image or story that leads one interpretation, then finish with a single line that flips the meaning (e.g., housekeeper banging on door → 'I had to get up and let her out'). Effective for physical images and act-outs; timing and delivery are critical to land the flip.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRIPLES
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-way build up: two seemingly logical items followed by a third absurd exaggeration that shatters the implied pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build tension with two normal items then break pattern with a punchy third. Examples: mock phobias list, or listing island outages then a vacationing Don King with flat hair. Useful for list-format jokes and one-liners.

rubrics_metrics.name: INCONGRUITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposing two dissimilar ideas into one idea (associative comedy), putting things together that normally don’t go together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly used to give human qualities to objects or to collide cultural/language expectations (e.g., 'Authentic Chinese Cuisine — Se Habla Espanol'). Works well as description, character act-out, or associative observation. Very widely used in contemporary comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: SIMPLE TRUTH
rubrics_metrics.description: Like double-entendre but uses phrases: take the implied truth of a phrase and state the literal or ‘simple’ truth for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use everyday phrases, lyrics, scripture or metaphor and reveal a literal or alternate interpretation (e.g., 'I remember the first time I had sex. It’s right there on my credit card statement.'). Short, crisp phrasing and timing help land the twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: SUPERIORITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage the audience to feel superior to silly thoughts or actions — via self-deprecation, attacking authority (cops, politicians), or mocking those who think they are better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the audience feel they’re 'in on it' by showing them someone’s foolishness. Can include character bits and put-downs; be aware of target sensitivity and delivery to avoid alienating the crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAIRED PHRASES
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilize the rhythms of antonyms, homonyms and synonyms — often presenting paradox or contrast in paired rhythms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallel structure and wordplay (e.g., HOPE/GROPE/DOPE or 'mildly pissed off for thirty-five') to create a rhythmic punch. Paradox within paired phrases is often rewarded by audience recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: SLAPSTICK
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical comedy and 'stupidity' performed as act-outs; broad physicality often reserved for sketch or live-action but can be used in stand-up as act-outs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physicalization (falling, exaggerated movements, facial expressions) to sell a joke. In stand-up, keep slapstick focused and purposeful (often as a tag or act-out) rather than prolonged sketch-level business.

rubrics_metrics.name: OBSERVATION-RECOGNITION
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify everyday behaviors, signs, commercials or routines and magnify them with a bit of exaggeration so the audience recognizes and laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target widely-shared experiences (e.g., plugging in a USB, removing cellophane, odd commercial claims). Include behaviors and act-outs to make the recognition physical; specificity and relatability are key. Examples: Cialis warning, Ex-Lax commercial, blowing your nose.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMPARE & CONTRAST
rubrics_metrics.description: Impose surprise by stating a complex or technical direction then pulling the rug out by responding with an oversimplified or literal conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up an expectation of sophistication or complexity then deflate it with a simple, blunt punchline (e.g., astrology/Capricorn gag). Use contrast to highlight absurdity and create a quick payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMEDIC IRONY
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dramatic irony: expression of meaning by using language that signifies the opposite or situations where the audience knows information characters do not; often subtle and discovery-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony can be subtle and puzzle-like; it usually brings a quieter reaction unless it's poignant or blatant. Ensure the audience has the necessary knowledge/context. Examples include Oedipus Rex-type situations and routines exposing hypocrisy (George Carlin, professor/priest examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: BENIGN RETALIATION
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy payback humor: imagining revenge or 'getting back' at someone without real harm — a comedic revenge that the audience can root for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences relate to vengeful fantasies (e.g., petty revenge on a spouse or ex). Draw from real-life slights and the 'what I should have said' moments. Reactions can vary depending on harshness and delivery; tailor severity to crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: PARADOX
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement that contradicts itself yet might be true; paradox often overlaps with incongruity and irony and produces laughter by cognitive inversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-contradictory but recognizably true statements (e.g., time described as distance and vice versa, 'my accountant sucks; he’s too honest'). Paradox engages both hemispheres of the listener’s brain and can elevate comedic sophistication. Short, crisp paradoxes are effective in one-liners and tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke structure: Setup – Punchline – Tag
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are constructed as setup → punchline → tag(s) (or act-out tag). Tags extend or escalate the laugh after the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember to include tags and toppers: after the punchline, add tags (one-liners or act-outs) to extend the laugh. An act-out is a tag that is physicalized; use tags to deepen or sharpen the original punch.
